tesis: Laughter isn't a response to humor: it's a social signal used to bond. Which is why you can be liked without telling a single joke.
notas_humor: Este episodio no necesita adaptación cultural: el estudio de Provine se hizo en centros comerciales y aceras estadounidenses, así que en inglés el ejemplo es memoria propia y no un caso extranjero. Se le deja el peso.

Las tres frases de la escena 6 se devuelven a su forma original en inglés (“Where have you been?”, “See you later”, “Are you sure you know what you're doing?”): son las que Provine transcribió, no una traducción de la traducción.
Gancho: el dato es tan contraintuitivo que hace de chiste él solo. No hay juego de palabras que pueda romperse al cambiar de idioma.
Escena 18: autoconciencia del formato, una sola vez en el vídeo, con remate seco (“a demonstration by absence”) en vez de la frase larga del original español.
Cierre: callback a la frase banal del principio.
Ortografía americana en todo el guion.

escenas.subtitulo: And there are twelve hundred recordings that prove it
escenas.narracion: In the nineteen nineties, a neuroscientist named Robert Provine got tired of studying laughter in a laboratory.

escenas.texto: So he went outside with a notebook.
escenas.narracion: So he did something strange for a scientist. He went out into the street with a notebook and started writing down every time he heard somebody laugh.

escenas.pie: episodes of spontaneous laughter logged in malls, sidewalks and hallways. Each one with the line that came _immediately before_
escenas.narracion: He collected around twelve hundred episodes of spontaneous laughter, in shopping malls, on sidewalks, in hallways. And for each one he recorded something nobody had recorded before: the exact sentence that came right before the laugh.

escenas.texto: The result doesn't fit anything you believe about laughing.
escenas.narracion: The result is one of those findings that rearranges your head.

escenas.pie: of the lines before a laugh were _remotely_ joke-like. The rest, nothing
escenas.narracion: Only around ten to twenty percent of those lines were even remotely joke-like. The rest — the overwhelming majority — weren't funny at all.

escenas.titulo: Real lines that got a laugh
puntos: “Are you sure you know what you're doing?”
escenas.narracion: We're talking about lines like “where have you been”, “see you later”, or “are you sure you know what you're doing”. Nobody would be laughing at that. And yet they were.

escenas.texto: So if they're not laughing at the *content*… at what?
escenas.narracion: Which leaves a fairly large question on the table. If people aren't laughing at what's being said, what are they laughing at?
The answer is that laughter, almost always, isn't a reaction to anything. It's a message.

escenas.texto: A message that says: _this is going fine between us_.
escenas.narracion: A very short and very old message, and roughly it says: whatever is happening between you and me is not a threat. We're good.

escenas.texto: And two findings give it away.
escenas.narracion: And there are two observations that make that pretty clear.

escenas.a: Laughs less. Even though the ending is a surprise to them.
escenas.b: Laughs _more_. And already knew the ending.
escenas.narracion: The first: in those recordings, the person speaking laughs considerably more than the person listening. If laughter were a response to content, it would have to be the other way around — the one telling it already knows the ending.

escenas.texto: Second: laughter never interrupts a sentence. It *punctuates* it.
escenas.narracion: The second is even cleaner. Laughter almost never shows up in the middle of a sentence. It shows up at the end, in the pauses, exactly where a period or a comma would go. Provine said laughter punctuates speech.

escenas.texto: If it were involuntary, it would land *wherever it wanted*.
escenas.narracion: Think about that. If it were an uncontrollable reaction, it would land wherever it liked. The fact that it respects grammar means something is managing it.
Although not all laughter is the same. There are two kinds, and your ear tells them apart even if you can't explain how.

escenas.a: Fires on its own. Higher, more irregular. Hard to fake.
escenas.b: You produce it on purpose. It sounds like *speech*.
escenas.narracion: One is spontaneous: it fires by itself, sounds higher and more irregular, and is very hard to imitate. The other is volitional: you produce it deliberately, like another word, and acoustically it resembles speech more than it resembles real laughter.

escenas.texto: Played to listeners in _24 societies_, they told them apart above chance.
escenas.narracion: And in one study, recordings of both were played to listeners in twenty-four different societies around the world. Above chance, they could tell which was which.

escenas.texto: A *sincerity detector* that works without a shared language.
escenas.narracion: Which means you are carrying around a fake-laugh detector that needs no common language. And it explains that uncomfortable feeling when somebody laughs at your joke a fraction too fast.

escenas.texto: Said by a voice that can produce *neither of them*.
escenas.narracion: Yes: this is being told to you by a voice that can produce neither. Call it a demonstration by absence.
And now the practical consequence, which is enormous and almost nobody draws it.

escenas.texto: If laughter is a *social signal*, the joke was never the target.
escenas.narracion: If laughter is mainly a bonding signal and not a grade on your content, then trying to be funny by telling jokes is attacking the problem from the hardest possible angle.

puntos: Shared reference: the thing only the two of you get
Permission: laugh first, and at yourself
escenas.narracion: What really produces laughter in a conversation is something else: being present and responding for real; building shared references, the ones only the two of you get; and giving permission, by laughing first and at your own expense.

escenas.texto: None of that needs a *joke*. All of it can be trained.
escenas.narracion: None of that requires a joke. And all of it is far easier to train than writing punchlines.
With one important warning, and it runs against the usual advice.

escenas.texto: *Volitional* laughter works too. But it shows.
escenas.narracion: Laughing on purpose to smooth a situation is legitimate and everybody does it. The problem is that, as we just saw, the other person detects it. Laughing at everything constantly doesn't make you seem warm: it makes you seem nervous.

escenas.texto: Laughter is *information*. Give it away free and it stops informing.
escenas.narracion: Laughter is information about what you approve of. Hand it out without discrimination and it stops meaning anything.

escenas.texto: Next time, notice what they said *just before*. Probably nothing.
escenas.narracion: So next time somebody laughs with you, notice what they said right before it. Odds are it was “see you later”.

escenas.titulo: You don't need *jokes*. You need presence.

escenas.narracion: Next episode: the four humor styles, and which one of them is costing you friends without you having noticed.
